title: A house of leaves
hookLine: the exiles reach the mountain, meet the poet telling their story, and bless a hut of leaves before stepping in
carry: griha pravesha: bless the home, then enter
last: A TIRTHA IS A HOLY CROSSING.

cards: The forest is in flower. Rama walks with Sita, and for the first time since Ayodhya, he sounds almost happy. Look, he tells her: the flame-of-the-forest trees are in bloom, so red they look on fire.
Honeycombs hang from the branches, big as buckets. Listen to the birds. Then the trees open, and there it is: a mountain with many peaks, streams running down its sides.

teach.b: Chitrakuta, or Chitrakoot as many say it today, means something like the bright peak, or the many-colored peak. Rama decides at once: we'll live here. But first, a visit.
On the mountain is the hermitage of a sage, and the three exiles bow to him. The sage is Valmiki.
Enjoy that for a second: the poet telling this whole story appears inside it, welcoming the hero he's writing about. Then the work.

teach.h: A PARNASHALA, A HOUSE OF LEAVES.
teach.b: Lakshmana gathers wood and leaves and builds a hut, a parnashala, a house of leaves, strong against wind and rain, with a door and a thatched roof.
And before anyone steps inside, Rama performs a rite to bless the house, with offerings to the gods of the dwelling. Only then do the three of them go in. Hindus still do this.

Before a family moves into a new home, there's often a griha pravesha, a house-entering: a puja or a havan, a lamp, a pot of water, in many families milk boiled over on the new stove, and only then does anyone sleep there.
The idea is simple and deep. A house isn't just walls.
It's a place where God is invited to live with you, and you invite God first.
Look how far this week has come: from a chariot leaving a weeping city, across two great rivers, to a house of leaves on a bright mountain, blessed before anyone stepped in.

how: Many Hindu families hold a griha pravesha, a house-entering ceremony, before moving into a new home; in the text, Rama blesses the leaf hut at Chitrakuta before the three exiles enter it.

o: a hermitage where the exiles stay only a single night
the bright mountain where the exiles make their first home
the capital city the exiles leave behind in tears

games.q: the bright peak — tap the pairs.
p: the poet who greets them on the mountain

s: Valmiki appears inside his own story
the exiles visit his hermitage on Chitrakuta.
the exiles move into the hut without any rite
Rama blesses the house before they enter, as for a new home.
Chitrakuta is a single bare rock
it's a mountain of many peaks, streams, birds and honey.

games.q: you're Rama. Lakshmana has finished the leaf hut, and it's getting dark. what comes before you step inside?
o: a rite to bless the home.
a feast for the sage next door.
games.why: Rama blesses the hut with offerings before the three of them enter, the way Hindu families still hold a griha pravesha.

practice: Picture one corner of the place you live, a chair, a window, a doorway, the way Rama and Sita saw their hut that first night: small, new and theirs.
If you pray, do what many Hindus do in a new home: picture a lamp lit in that corner, and ask God to live there with you.
If you don't, breathe in gratitude for a roof, and breathe out the same wish for someone who doesn't have one.

wordCard.voice: Chitrakoot. The bright mountain where the exiles meet Valmiki, and Rama blesses a house of leaves before they make it their first home in the forest.

orig.note: Sanskrit parṇaśālā: a hut of leaves, parṇa (leaf) plus śālā (hall, house); the exiles' home on Chitrakuta.

carryVoice: Your line: griha pravesha: bless the home, then enter. Small, new, and blessed before anyone stepped in. That's day five hundred thirty-nine.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 56 (the walk to Chitrakuta; meeting Valmiki; the leaf hut and its blessing)
